Micro-computed tomography confirmed homogeneous random packing, with filler volume fractions of 35–56% depending on geometry. Compressive testing across 51 specimens showed filler geometry is the dominant reinforcement determinant: tetrapods achieve up to 12-fold stiffening and a packing-normalised modulus of 65.8 MPa, outperforming cubes despite lower filler volume. Critically, 1 mm 3 cubic fillers display a reproducible non-monotonic stress plateau absent in all tetrapod specimens, consistent with contact-chain buckling within the densely packed network. Post-compression analysis reveals an orthogonal failure hierarchy: matrix stiffness governs deformation magnitude while filler geometry independently governs failure topology. As a vision demonstration, tetrapod fillers were volumetrically printed in a PEGDA hydrogel trabecular scaffold, opening a path towards tissue engineering scaffold applications. This study establishes, to our knowledge, the first systematic framework for geometry-dependent mechanical characterisation of sub-millimetre architected fillers in soft composites.

title: 57Fe-enriched iron oxide nanoparticles as tracers in hydrated biomimetic matrices: interfacial effects and measurement constraints
abstract: Selective analysis of iron oxide nanoparticles in soft and hydrated matrices remains challenging due to the lack of specificity of conventional analytical techniques and interference from background iron. Here, we present an isotopically engineered iron oxide nanoparticle platform that enables isotope-specific detection and phase-resolved analysis under biologically relevant conditions. Iron oxide nanoparticles enriched in 57 Fe were synthesized and systematically characterized. Their spectral response was investigated in model environments to assess nanoparticle–matrix interfacial effects. Mössbauer measurements revealed a pronounced temperature-dependent loss of magnetic spectral area, accompanied by broadening and distortion of the hyperfine-field distribution, indicating increasing contributions from dynamically relaxing nanoparticles. These observations demonstrate that isotope-specific detection allows identification of nanoparticle-derived iron and enables analysis of phase composition without interference from non-labeled iron species. However, nanoparticle mobility and matrix–particle interactions impose fundamental limitations on reliable Mössbauer measurements. We quantify temperature-dependent signal loss and line-shape distortions associated with nanoparticle motion. These findings provide practical guidelines for Mössbauer measurements of mobile nanoparticle systems and support the potential use of isotope-specific approaches for nanoparticle tracking and characterization in biologically relevant environments.

title: Advances in EB PVD thermal barrier coatings: materials and processing innovations for CMAS resistance in aero engine applications
abstract: Electron-beam physical vapor deposition (EB-PVD) thermal barrier coatings protect aero-engine hot-section components while accommodating cyclic strain through their separated columnar architecture. However, the connected gaps and feather-like substructures also provide pathways for molten calcia–magnesia–alumino–silicate (CMAS) deposits derived from ingested environmental particles. Infiltration couples coating dissolution and phase evolution to reduced optical scattering, increased stiffness, and interfacial damage, undermining thermal insulation and cyclic durability. This review synthesizes materials and processing innovations using a transport–reaction–fracture framework that emphasizes the architecture-specific requirements of EB-PVD systems. Deposit chemistry, particle thermal history, wetting, and column-network topology are linked to the timing and location of infiltration, crystallization, and failure. Yttria-rich zirconia, rare-earth zirconates, garnet-forming aluminates, phosphates, reactive oxide overlays, and emerging multicomponent ceramics are assessed alongside laser surface modification, column refinement, and multilayer designs. The synthesis identifies a common design requirement: protection must restrict connected liquid transport before vulnerable regions are reached without producing a brittle cap or weakening internal interfaces. Favorable reaction products and low penetration depths are therefore evaluated against coating consumption, retained thermal resistance, compliance, and cyclic integrity. A proposed multiscale modeling workflow connects thermodynamic and infiltration analyses to fracture and component-level exposure, while distinguishing mechanistic screening from coating-system validation. Priorities include comparable deposit and thermal histories, repeated melting and deposition, and functional measurements beyond post-exposure penetration depth. The resulting design rules favor localized reactive protection, controlled column-gap connectivity, and a compliant underlying coating, providing a basis for translating laboratory mitigation strategies into reproducible and repairable aero-engine coating systems.

title: Elucidating the factors governing strength–plasticity synergy in B2-containing bulk metallic glass composites
abstract: The mechanical properties of in situ bulk metallic glass (BMG) composites depend on multiple characteristics of the crystalline second phase, whose individual contributions are difficult to distinguish. Here, the coupled roles of four factors were examined in TiZrCuNiSiSn BMG composites: (i) second-phase fraction, (ii) phase transformation behavior, (iii) second-phase distribution, and (iv) amorphous-matrix enclosure. Compression tests and in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction provided insights into how these factors jointly influence deformation. First, the B2-phase fraction was associated with the plastic-deformation mode, with increasing fractions reducing the stress drops associated with collective shear-band motion. Second, the B2 transformation behavior was closely associated with plasticity: a lower transformation stress enhanced plasticity, whereas its effect on yield strength depended on the degree of constraint imposed by the surrounding amorphous matrix. Third, in both the isolated and interconnected B2 microstructures, martensitic transformation first became detectable at approximately 1.7 GPa, indicating that the transformation was delayed until a similarly high stress level. Fourth, the sharp strength decrease at high B2 fractions was interpreted in terms of a local loss of amorphous matrix enclosure, which may reduce constraint on the surface-exposed B2 regions and increase the influence of their transformation on macroscopic yielding. These findings suggest that incorporating a low-transformation-stress B2 phase while maintaining sufficient constraint through amorphous-matrix enclosure is an effective strategy for achieving both high strength and large plasticity.

title: Numerical simulation of tensile behavior of MICP precipitates with an extended multiphase particle placement algorithm
abstract: Microbially Induced Calcium Carbonate Precipitation (MICP) is a promising green solidification technique, but its complex mesostructure limits its tensile performance. This study investigates the mesostructure-tensile response relationship in multiphase MICP precipitates. We developed an efficient multiphase particle-placement framework where a deterministic mapping converts phase fractions to particle numbers, followed by stochastic non-overlapping spatial placement. The generated geometry is coupled with a cohesive zone model (CZM) to simulate crack initiation, propagation, and coalescence under tensile loading. Experimental tensile tests on MICP-bonded mortar provide reference data on strength, brittleness, and failure characteristics. A representative CZM parameter set is adopted to provide a physically reasonable strength level and brittle softening response for the subsequent comparative parametric analyses. Parametric analyses reveal that the effective elastic modulus is highly sensitive to crystal phase composition and follows Voigt-Reuss bounds, whereas tensile strength is primarily governed by the amorphous matrix and interface properties. Increasing particle size enhances stress concentration, resulting in reduced tensile strength and more brittle behavior. These findings provide model-based insights into how interface properties and crystallization characteristics may influence the tensile response of MICP precipitates and demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework for comparative analysis of heterogeneous composite materials

title: Shell-based numerical identification of effective transverse shear stiffness for thin-walled sections: isotropic steel benchmarks
abstract: Effective transverse shear stiffness is a key parameter in reduced-order modelling of thin-walled members, particularly when complex cross-sectional geometries prevent reliable closed-form evaluation. This study develops a shell-based framework and compares three identification procedures using isotropic steel benchmarks: global compliance, volume-integrated transverse shear energy, and sectional shear fields. Eight open and closed cross-sections are examined in 114 numerical configurations, including variations of length, thickness, mesh size, sectional sampling position, end loading, and the local shell shear coefficient. Both transverse beam shear components are retained in the energy measures. Sectional estimates differ from elementary rectangular and circular thin-wall references by 0.040% and 0.024%, respectively, on the investigated 2 mm meshes. For the Sigma-section, refinement from 2 to 1 mm changes the sectional estimate by 0.136%, compared with 4.85% for global compliance identification. Longitudinal scans and alternative loading show that a stable central value does not by itself establish independence from the benchmark configuration. The framework distinguishes numerical consistency, spatial field development, and sensitivity to coupled deformation, providing qualified criteria for transferring shell-model information to reduced beam representations

title: Cellular grain control for enhanced pitting resistance in LPBF NiTi alloys
abstract: We report a strategy to enhance the pitting corrosion resistance of Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) NiTi alloys by tailoring the cellular grain (CG) proportion via melt pool density control. A low laser power (80 W) and scanning speed (480 mm/s) increase the number of melt pools, followed by intermediate annealing to relieve residual stress. The resulting ASL sample exhibits a high CG proportion of 41.2% with reduced micro-strain. The ASL sample shows pronounced repassivation and an extended passive region up to ~1800 mV, which is 1.2~9 times wider than those of most reported NiTi alloys, indicating significantly improved pitting resistance. This enhancement is attributed to the high proportion of submicron cellular grains combined with low micro-strain, which promote the formation of a dense and regenerative TiO2-dominated passive film, thereby improving resistance to chloride-induced corrosion. Notably, net-like Ti4Ni2Ox nanoprecipitates distributed along the cellular grain boundaries contribute to the initial metastable pits but do not dominate the long-term corrosion behavior. These findings highlight the critical role of microstructural design in regulating passivation behavior and provide a strategy for developing corrosion-resistant LPBF NiTi alloys.

title: Nonlinear hyper-viscoelastic modeling of first harmonic response in CB-reinforced SSBRs using LAOS: Study of Payne effect and molecular weight distribution
abstract: This study develops a mathematical modeling framework to analyze the Large Amplitude Oscillatory Shear (LAOS) behavior of carbon black (CB)-reinforced solution styrene–butadiene rubbers (SSBRs), focusing on the Payne effect and molecular weight distribution (MWD). Two SSBR grades with distinct MWDs and CB loadings (0, 30, 50, and 70 phr) were investigated. A nonlinear hyper-viscoelastic constitutive model based on a Zener-type formulation, incorporating the Mullins effect, was employed to capture filler–polymer interactions under large strain amplitudes. Experimental data were obtained using a Rubber Processing Analyzer, and model validation was performed using first harmonic storage and loss moduli. In addition, auxiliary experiments, including filler dispersion analysis and bound rubber content (BRC) measurements, were conducted to further support the interpretation of the results. The findings indicate that CB content, MWD, and Mooney viscosity strongly influence the Payne effect, with distinct trends across formulations. The model accurately captures the nonlinear viscoelastic response and provides insights for optimizing tire compound performance. A limitation of this study is the exclusive use of first harmonic data, which may not fully represent higher-order nonlinearities inherent in LAOS behavior.

title: In-depth mechanistic study of the oxidative dissolution of uranium dioxide under water radiolysis using oxygen isotopes and studtite’s Raman spectra
abstract: Understanding the oxidative dissolution mechanisms of uranium dioxide under water radiolysis is a major challenge in the context of the underwater storage of spent nuclear fuels. This study proposes an original approach using oxygen isotopes to better understand the role of radiolytic species in uranium oxidation and alteration product formation at the atomic scale. To this end, we studied an isotopically labeled reaction interface (U18O2/H216O), which was subjected to gamma irradiation and, consequently, to water radiolysis, using Raman spectroscopy. For the first time, the production of labeled U18O2 pellets was successfully achieved according to an original method via hydroxide precipitation. Leaching experiments were conducted in aerated, unlabeled water under external gamma irradiation (dose rate of 750 Gy.h-1) to produce oxidizing species and induce the precipitation of studtite (UO2)(O2)(H2O)2(H2O)2. Additionally, leaching experiments with the simple addition of H216/18O2 were carried out. Comparing the results revealed the respective roles of radicals and hydrogen peroxide in forming the uranyl ion and the origin of the peroxo ligands in studtite. The free OH° radicals appear to contribute mainly to the oxidation of uranium. Meanwhile, the peroxo ligands that link the uranyl ions in studtite appear to originate from the hydrogen peroxide in solution.

title: AI-driven identification of key roughness-related descriptors for electrical contact resistance
abstract: This paper investigates the effect of surface roughness parameters on the electrical contact resistance (ECR) in fuel cells. Despite extensive efforts, the effect of roughness on ECR remains poorly understood, mainly because roughness is commonly only characterized by the arithmetic mean height. This work proposes a comprehensive set of parameters spanning amplitude, lateral spatial distribution, and summit density metrics to investigate their influence on ECR at various external pressures. Numerically generated rough surfaces are brought into contact with compliant counter-surfaces. Random Forest regression quantifies their pressure-dependent importance, and SHAP analysis reveals the direction and magnitude of their effects. Three pressure-dependent regimes, each dominated by a different descriptor, are identified. At the onset of contact (0.1 MPa), the solidity factor, which characterizes the balance between peaks and valleys, dominates. Between 0.1 and 2.2 MPa, the autocorrelation length dictates the dependence of ECR on pressure, while above 2.2 MPa, ECR saturates and is controlled by the summit density. These results provide a unified interpretation of previously conflicting studies and demonstrate the necessity of multi-descriptor roughness characterization to understand its impact on ECR.

title: Engineering colloidal homogeneity for Grain-Growth restriction in transparent Al2O3–Si3N4 nanocomposites
abstract: Transparent alumina ceramics require the simultaneous optimization of optical transparency and mechanical reliability; however, nanoparticle reinforcement is often limited by incomplete dispersion and microstructural heterogeneity. This study develops a processing–structure–property framework, termed Global Zener Pinning (GZP), for transparent Al 2 O 3 –Si 3 N 4 nanocomposites based on a processing-oriented colloidal-engineering approach, in which colloidal homogeneity is considered an important factor influencing the practical effectiveness of nanoparticle-assisted grain-growth restriction. A systematic colloidal-engineering route combining dispersant and pH optimization, magnetized-water treatment, ultrasonication, and controlled drying was employed before spark plasma sintering. The optimized condition produced a mean grain size of 380 nm and a relative density of 99.57%, together with Vickers hardness of 17.80 GPa and flexural strength of 415.24 MPa, compared with 14.70 GPa and 360.02 MPa, respectively, for the conventionally processed Al 2 O 3 –0.1 wt% Si 3 N 4 condition, while the Weibull modulus increased from 4.7 for monolithic α-Al 2 O 3 to 16 for the optimized condition. Infrared transmittance reached approximately 85% in the 5–6 μm region. Regression analysis further established quantitative relationships among selected mechanical descriptors within the experimental domain. The results demonstrate the practical significance of colloidal architecture in influencing grain refinement and multifunctional performance.

title: StampFormer: A physics-guided material-geometry-coupled multimodal model for rapid prediction of physical fields in sheet metal stamping
abstract: Traditional sheet metal forming relies on computationally expensive Finite Element Analysis (FEA), significantly prolonging design cycles. While surrogate models accelerate iteration, existing approaches either provide limited scalar outputs or ignore crucial material properties by focusing solely on geometry. To address this gap, we develop StampFormer, a physics-guided deep learning framework that simultaneously processes component geometry and material stress-strain responses to predict FEA outcomes. Its architecture employs a Material-Augmented Geometric Network (MAGN) for initial multimodal fusion, followed by a Hierarchical Material Embedding Injection Unit (HMEIU) that progressively integrates material features into an adapted Swin-UNet backbone. Evaluated on steel and aluminium crossmember stamping datasets, StampFormer predicts critical physical fields—including thinning, major/minor strain, plastic strain, and displacement—in under a second. Compared with the reference FEA, our model achieves a mean representative-maximum relative error below for each of the four 2D fields in both material datasets and a masked displacement mean squared error below mm 2 . Within the investigated component family and fixed process conditions, this multimodal framework provides sub-second predictions for rapid early-stage material–geometry screening and design exploration.

title: Divergent microstructural pathways under comparable initial creep kinetics in Inconel 617
abstract: A critical challenge in ensuring the long-term reliability of Inconel 617 (IN617) for advance ultra-supercritical (A-USC) applications is determining whether comparable macroscopic creep responses under different stress–temperature conditions arise from identical microstructural deformation mechanisms. To address this, the creep behaviour of IN617 was investigated at intermediate temperatures (750–800 °C) under applied stresses of 160–280 MPa. Creep testing combined with EBSD, TEM, STEM–EDS and SXRD compared two conditions (750 °C–240 MPa and 800 °C–160 MPa) with comparable initial creep strain rates. Increasing temperature and stress accelerated creep deformation, reducing creep life and raising minimum creep rates. Despite similar initial creep responses, the two conditions evolved through fundamentally different microstructural pathways. The 750 °C–240 MPa condition was dominated by sustained dislocation activity, high dislocation density and precipitate shearing, whereas the 800 °C–160 MPa condition exhibited enhanced recovery and recrystallisation associated with stronger precipitate–dislocation interactions from additional carbide precipitation and probable fine-scale γ′ evolution. These findings show that similar macroscopic creep responses can arise through fundamentally different microstructural pathways, providing new mechanistic insight into intermediate-temperature creep of IN617 and a stronger basis for creep-life prediction and component design in advanced high-temperature applications.

title: Machining-induced surface integrity and early cellular response in anisotropic cortical bone
abstract: Machined bone surfaces constitute the initial interface for cell attachment during bone healing and implant fixation. Although cortical bone anisotropy strongly influences material removal during machining, its effect on the relationship between machining-induced surface topography and early cellular response remains poorly understood. In this paper, side milling was performed on bovine cortical bone along the parallel, across, and transverse osteonal directions using different feed levels. Surface integrity was characterized using three-dimensional roughness measurements and scanning electron microscopy, and the biological response was evaluated by culturing human mesenchymal stem cells on the machined surfaces to assess their proliferation index over 21 days. Increasing feed from to increased arithmetic mean height from to parallel to osteons, to across osteons, and to transverse to osteons, while producing more negative skewness, higher kurtosis, and fracture damage. However, the low-feed across condition yielded the highest proliferation index, -fold the parallel value and -fold the transverse value at the same feed. An exploratory regression with surface amplitude, skewness, kurtosis, and cutting direction explained of day-21 variation. These findings position machining-induced surface integrity, not roughness amplitude only, as a key engineering criterion for biologically informed bone-surface preparation.

title: Coupled nitride and oxide precipitation at intergranular cracks in a creep-deformed γ-γ’ superalloy
abstract: The ductility drop of polycrystalline nickel-based superalloys at high temperature is often considered to originate from the fracture of grain boundary oxides formed by stress-assisted grain boundary oxidation (SAGBO). In this report, we show that nitrides also form ahead of the oxide front. In a polycrystalline γ-γ’ superalloy processed by additive manufacturing and deformed under creep at 700 °C and 690 MPa, in a region > 1 µm ahead of a cracked and oxidized grain boundary, a high density of (Cr,Ti)N nitrides is found at dislocations and γ-γ’ interfaces. The chemistry and structure of the nitrides is evidenced with a combination of transmission electron microscopy techniques and atom probe tomography. The formation of nitrides, in addition to that of the already characterized oxides, is expected to locally harden the material and enhance the cracking susceptibility of grain boundaries during creep.

title: Oxidation resistant refractory complex lean alloy with excellent compressive formability
abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys are known for their poor room temperature compressive formability, high temperature oxidation resistance and density while exhibiting substantial strength at room and elevated temperatures. In line with that, a low density Nb 70 Ti 15 Mo 2 W 1.5 Ta 0.5 Al 10 Cr 1 complex lean alloy (Cr-1 CLA) is presented in the current work which exhibited excellent room temperature compressive strength-formability synergy while undergoing very controlled isothermal oxidation at 1000°C for 24 hrs exposure. This controlled oxidation in Cr-1 CLA is attributed to the formation of less permeable complex Nb-rich oxide layers (containing Al and Cr) at the surface thereby limiting the weight gain to 43.48 mg/cm 2 upon exposure at 1000°C for 24 hrs. The improved compressive strength-formability synergy is a result of sustained work hardening at RT owing to two phase strengthening dominated deformation. Thus, the design of Cr-1 CLA opens a new pathway for realizing the light-weight refractory complex alloys overcoming the conventional oxidation concerns when exposed to higher temperature applications.

title: A multifunctional nanozyme for modulating the tumor microenvironment to synergistically enhance cancer treatment
abstract: The tumor microenvironment (TME) is characterized by elevated glutathione (GSH) levels and hypoxia, two interrelated pathological features that synergistically contribute to radioresistance. Conventional nanozymes, however, are constrained by intrinsically low catalytic efficiency, limited functional versatility, and inadequate biocompatibility, key limitations that collectively hinder their clinical translation. To overcome these barriers, we developed a hyaluronic acid-modified Pt@MnO 2 -Au-HA nanozyme with a well-defined core–shell–satellite architecture: a platinum (Pt) core, a conformal MnO 2 interlayer, and spatially controlled gold (Au) nanoparticle satellites. Following intravenous administration, Pt@MnO 2 -Au-HA selectively targets proinflammatory macrophages in the tumor microenvironment via hyaluronic acid–mediated CD44 receptor recognition. Within the tumor, endogenously overexpressed hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) is catalytically decomposed into oxygen (O 2 ) by the MnO 2 component, which exhibits intrinsic catalase (CAT)-like activity. This O 2 generation serves as an endogenous oxygen source to enhance glucose depletion via the glucose oxidase (GOx)-like activity of the Au component, thereby enabling starvation therapy. Concurrently, elevated intratumoral GSH induces the reductive dissolution of MnO 2 , resulting in both GSH consumption and controlled release of the Pt core. The liberated Pt nanoparticles further exert CAT-like activity to convert H 2 O 2 into O 2 , effectively alleviating tumor hypoxia and synergistically amplifying radiotherapy efficacy through enhanced radiosensitization.

title: Distinct precipitation pathways in NiAlY oxidation under dry and humid CO2 conditions
abstract: The oxidation resistance of Ni-based alloys relies on forming a protective Al2O3 scale, yet the effects of complex environments like humid CO2 on microstructural evolution remain unclear. This study reveals that while oxidation of a Y-doped NiAl alloy at 950 °C in dry and humid CO2 produces similar oxide scale thickness and a γ-Al2O3/α-Al2O3 bilayer structure, the internal microstructure and precipitate chemistry differ significantly. In dry CO2, the scale is porous and defective, with metallic Ni–Y-rich precipitates and localized Y segregation, which may compromise long-term stability. In contrast, humid CO2 yields a dense, well-adhered scale with uniformly distributed Y and NiAl2O4 spinel precipitates, driven by higher oxygen activity. The exclusion of Y from spinel is attributed to ionic radius mismatch and unfavorable charge compensation. These findings highlight the critical role of water vapor in improving scale integrity and reactive element distribution, offering guidance for designing oxidation-resistant alloys for high-temperature, moisture-rich environments.

title: Loading-mode-dependent energy absorption in TPU/recycled rubber blends: from viscoelastic damping to perforation resistance
abstract: Incorporating recycled rubber into thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) is a promising route to create sustainable damping materials. However, the relationship between viscoelastic properties and energy absorption remains poorly understood. Injection-molded TPU blends containing ground tire rubber (GTR), devulcanized GTR (dGTR), and sulfur- and peroxide-cured thermoplastic dynamic vulcanizates (TDVs) were characterized at 30–60 wt% rubber content by dynamic mechanical analysis, perforation testing, and repeated low-energy falling weight impact testing. DMA revealed a monotonic increase in viscoelastic damping with rubber content. dGTR exceeded GTR at equivalent loadings due to enhanced chain-segment mobility following devulcanization, whereas TDVs exhibited lower loss factors. Under perforation, increased damping did not translate into improved energy absorption: perforation resistance was more strongly associated with interfacial adhesion than with viscoelastic properties. The peroxide-cured TDV maintained near-matrix perforation resistance, while dGTR blends showed the largest reductions. Repeated low-energy impact tests showed that dissipated energy increased with rubber content and followed a similar composition-dependent trend to tanδ max , suggesting that viscoelastic damping contributes to energy dissipation. Tear strength measurements supported a deformation-mode-dependent interpretation: perforation is interface-controlled, while hysteresis dissipation is enhanced by partial interfacial debonding. The peroxide-cured TDV provided the most balanced performance in terms of puncture resistance and repeated-impact energy dissipation.

title: Engineering facet–defect coupling in 1D ZnO nanostructures for H2-rich syngas production during CO2 electroreduction
abstract: Understanding how synthesis conditions govern the structure and catalytic response of oxide nanostructures is essential for the rational design of efficient electrocatalysts for CO 2 conversion. Here, Zn/ZnO films were fabricated by thermal oxidation of Zn foils under static-air and flowing-air atmospheres, enabling the controlled growth of filamentary one-dimensional ZnO nanostructures with distinct morphologies, crystallographic textures and defect populations. Correlative X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, photoluminescence and electrochemical analyses reveal that the oxidation atmosphere drives the evolution of morphology while simultaneously regulating facet–defect coupling through the preferential formation of oxygen-defective ( 10 1 ¯ 1 ) facets. These coupled structural features strongly influence the competition between the CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) and the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), thereby determining the composition of the generated syngas. In particular, the sample grown under flowing air at 425 °C delivers the highest H 2 -rich syngas output, with an H 2 /CO ratio of ∼ 14, which correlates with the strongest oxygen-vacancy-related photoluminescence signature and the enhanced exposure of ( 10 1 ¯ 1 ) facets. These findings establish a clear processing–structure–property relationship in which growth atmosphere governs morphology, crystallographic orientation and defect chemistry to regulate proton adsorption, active-site competition and catalytic selectivity. Overall, this work identifies atmosphere-controlled facet–defect coupling as an effective strategy for engineering ZnO electrocatalysts toward H 2 -rich syngas production via CO 2 electroreduction.

title: BRNPs/SiO2 mixture for treating radiation-induced skin injury via alleviating oxidative stress and promoting skin repair
abstract: Radiation-induced skin injury (RISI) is one of the most common forms of tissue damage associated with radiotherapy and radiation exposure, facing a significant clinical challenge. Although natural products possess potent antioxidant and anti–inflammatory activities for radiation damage repair, their practical application is often limited by poor stability and low bioavailability. In this study, we constructed a natural product-derived self-assembled nanoparticle system (BRNPs) using resveratrol (Res) and berberine (BBR) to enhance cellular uptake and biocompatibility. A combined therapeutic system (BRNPs/SiO 2 mixture) was developed for the treatment of RISI by combining BRNPs with SiO 2 nanoparticles (SiO 2 NPs). BRNPs/SiO 2 mixture effectively scavenged intracellular ROS, reduced DNA damage and induced macrophage polarization toward the pro-regenerative M2 phenotype in vitro . In addition, this system markedly enhanced the cell migration of irradiated fibroblasts, endothelial tube formation and angiogenesis in vitro , thereby attenuating radiation-induced injury, accelerating wound healing and restoring skin barrier function in irradiated tissues of the RISI mouse model in vivo . These findings exhibited effective treatment of RISI via a combined strategy combining natural product-based nanomedicine and inorganic material.

title: Investigating process-dependent fracture energy in 3D-printed ABS using essential work of fracture: The role of nozzle temperature and print speed
abstract: In this study, the fracture behavior of additively manufactured polymers is strongly governed by process-induced microstructural features; however, the mechanisms governing crack initiation and propagation remain poorly understood. The influence of printing parameters, including printing speed and nozzle temperature, on the fracture behavior of 3D-printed acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) is methodically suggested employing the essential work of fracture (EWF) method. The results show that increasing nozzle temperature enhances crack initiation resistance up to around 15 %. In addition, higher printing speed promotes increased fracture energy (approximately14 %), indicating enhanced energy dissipation prior to failure. The present findings offer novel perspectives on the processing–structure–fracture relationships in additively manufactured ABS and demonstrate the effectiveness of the EWF method for characterizing fracture behavior.

title: SimuTDS: A new machine learning-based toolkit for simulating hydrogen desorption spectra
abstract: Hydrogen trapping at nanosized carbides influences hydrogen retention and embrittlement in high-strength steels, while interpretation of overlapping thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) peaks remains challenging. This study presents SimuTDS, an integrated apparent-kinetics and machine-learning framework for reconstructing TDS spectra and predicting apparent hydrogen desorption activation energies in ferritic and martensitic steels containing Ti-based carbides. Experimental validation and atomic-scale characterization were performed using a Ti-containing martensitic steel with a nominal composition of 0.04C-1.3Mn-0.1Si-0.11Ti wt.%. SimuTDS reconstructs spectra through convolution of apparent desorption contributions using a single heating-rate dataset, while machine-learning models incorporate TDS parameters, alloy composition, matrix microstructure, carbide coherency, and heat-treatment conditions to predict apparent desorption activation energies. The database comprised experimentally reported peak-level data from ferritic and martensitic Ti-carbide-containing steels. Bagged ensemble trees provided the highest predictive performance, with R 2 = 0.97. Atom-probe tomography revealed a near-stoichiometric Ti/C ratio at coherent TiC interfaces, whereas incoherent interfaces were locally carbon deficient. First-principles calculations showed that carbon-deficient interfaces provide energetically favourable sites for hydrogen accommodation. Coherent carbides were mainly associated with shallow trapping, whereas incoherent carbides exhibited broader and higher-energy desorption responses. For the investigated (Nb,V)C-containing reference dataset, comparison with an Oriani-based simulator showed larger discrepancies in reproducing the high-temperature desorption response than the lower-temperature peaks. Taken together, SimuTDS links TDS reconstruction, machine-learning prediction, and carbide-interface characteristics for interpreting hydrogen trapping in Ti-containing steels.

title: Trace Si regulation of phase competition enables strength–conductivity synergy in heat-treatment-free die-cast aluminum alloys
abstract: To overcome the strength–conductivity–castability trade-off in die-cast Al alloys for battery thermal management systems (BTMS), we developed a heat-treatment-free Al-Ce-Mg-Si alloy. CALPHAD-coupled Scheil simulations and hot cracking index calculations identified an optimal composition window: Al-9.8Ce-3.0Mg-XSi. Three alloys with 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 wt.% Si were fabricated by high-pressure die casting (HPDC). The 0.2Si alloy delivered the best balance: 194 MPa UTS, 90.2 MPa YS, 4.2% elongation, 146 W/(m·K) thermal conductivity, and 40 %IACS electrical conductivity. Microstructural analysis reveals Si governs phase evolution: at 0.1 wt.% Si, Mg2Si is too scarce for strengthening; at 0.2 wt.% Si, fine AlCeSi forms and promotes nanoscale Mg2Si and Guinier–Preston (GP) zones—enhancing strength without compromising ductility or conductivity; at 0.3 wt.% Si, coarse AlCeSi and Mg2Si induce interfacial defects that scatter phonons/electrons and initiate cracks—reducing plasticity, thermal conductivity, and electrical conductivity. First-principles calculations show Si binds more strongly to Ce than to Mg, suppressing Mg2Si nucleation and minimizing scattering. AlCeSi also exhibits higher Fermi-level density of states (DOS) and superior band dispersion near the Fermi level versus Mg2Si—enabling greater electron mobility and conductivity contribution. This work offers a direct route to high-strength, high-conductivity die-cast Al alloys for new energy vehicles.

title: Laser co-sintering of dissimilar ceramic heterostructures through temperature gradient control and hybrid laser manufacturing
abstract: Ceramic heterostructures integrating multiple ceramic materials via well-defined interfaces are promising for microelectronics, advanced sensing, and energy storage. However, co-sintering dissimilar ceramic phases with mismatched sintering characteristics in one step, without compositional compromise and with robust interfacial bonding, remains challenging. Herein, a multi-laser hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing technology is proposed, where the final CO 2 -laser step enables one-step co-sintering of Al 2 O 3 -BaTiO 3 ceramic heterostructures with in-plane complexity. A dual-layer green body was first printed by a doctor-blade, then micro-machined into the designed geometries using a femtosecond laser. The green body was then sintered into an Al 2 O 3 -BaTiO 3 heterostructure through a single CO 2 -laser co-sintering. By varying laser processing parameters and layer thickness, the control mechanism of laser co-sintering was systematically investigated. The experimental results show that the co-sintering outcome is jointly governed by laser energy input and layer geometry. Thermal simulations further suggest that this behavior is associated with a through-thickness temperature gradient, which can place the two ceramic layers within different temperature ranges compatible with their respective sintering behavior. Consequently, interfacial delamination resistance and structural stability were significantly enhanced. Moreover, complex Al 2 O 3 -BaTiO 3 heterostructures with various geometries were successfully fabricated, demonstrating a temperature-gradient-based framework for additive-free co-sintering of dissimilar ceramic heterostructures.

title: Residual stress in LPBF 316L specimens: equilibrium-consistent reconstruction from neutron diffraction measurements, size scaling, and texture effects
abstract: In this study, residual stresses (RS) in laser powder bed fused (LPBF) 316L steel cylinders were investigated to characterize their spatial distributions and dependence on specimen dimensions. Neutron diffraction (ND) was used to measure internal lattice strains, with particular emphasis on determining a stress-free lattice spacing, d 0 required to reconstruct stress fields consistent with global mechanical equilibrium. The reconstruction procedure employed area-averaged values of d 0 and enforced integral force equilibrium by applying small strain corrections within the experimental uncertainty. Near-surface stresses, which are important for satisfying equilibrium, are difficult to evaluate in cylindrical specimens using a conventional rotational ND setup because of limited spatial resolution and surface curvature. Complementary ND sin 2 ψ measurements on an LPBF plate, with a minimum measurement depth of 0.15 mm, were therefore used to characterize the near-surface stresses and guide extrapolation of the cylinder stress profiles to the free surface. The reconstructed stress distributions were independently validated by a sectioning experiment, in which the ND-derived stress profiles accurately predicted the specimen deflection induced by cutting. The effects of crystallographic texture, grain morphology, and elastic anisotropy on RS evaluation were also assessed using EBSD-informed self-consistent calculations

title: A density-dependent Drucker–Prager cap model for green powder compacts: identification, LS-DYNA user-material implementation and benchmark validation
abstract: Die-compaction calibrations are published as functions of relative density, yet production cap cards freeze every constant at one reference state. A modified Drucker–Prager Cap model is identified with every constant a function of density and each law’s form selected rather than assumed. On two contrasting powders, a diffusion-alloyed iron and a WC–Co hard metal, the selection proves material dependent, and both require an offset power law absent from the customary family. The model is implemented in LS-DYNA as a user material. Two findings reach beyond it. The density driving the laws must be the current one, advanced from the total volumetric strain: the plastic density costs up to of the closed-die stress. The constant mapping is exact for *MAT_025 but not for *MAT_159 , on which a transferred calibration overstates the ferrous closed-die axial stress by . At the material point the user material reproduces the instrumented-die record to at every tested density, where both stock cards fail. Applied without recalibration to the Dienet Case Study 2 benchmark, it reproduces the hub green densities to ; the upper and outer-lower punch loads stay and below the measurement, and all seven implementations of the benchmark fall further short.

title: Wharton’s jelly ECM containing sulfated alginate enhances chondrogenic differentiation of human adipose-derived stem cells for cartilage tissue engineering
abstract: Recently, Wharton’s jelly (WJ) has gained attention as a potential scaffold material for cartilage tissue engineering (CTE) due to its similarity to articular cartilage components, as well as its comparable structure and function to cartilage. This study reports the fabrication of decellularized WJ-ECM /alginate sulfate (ECM-ALGS) hybrid scaffolds to serve as a bioactive platform that supports chondrogenic differentiation of human adipose-derived stem cells (hADSCs). Moreover, the effects of alginate sulfate ratio on scaffold physical and biological properties were investigated. The results demonstrated that the ECM-ALGS scaffolds possessed appropriate biodegradation, hydrophilicity, and mechanical properties compared to pure WJ-ECM (ECM-ALGS-0) samples. The MTT assay and SEM images of the hADSCs seeded on scaffolds indicated the appropriate attachment and spreading of cells, respectively. The presence of chondrogenic proteins, notably type II collagen and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), was verified through Alcian blue staining and immunohistochemical analysis over a 14-day culture period, underscoring the contributory role of alginate sulfate in guiding cell differentiation. Furthermore, RT-PCR results confirmed the chondrogenic commitment of hADSCs cultured on ECM-ALGS scaffolds, as evidenced by the upregulated expression of type II collagen and aggrecan. Collectively, these observations highlight the suitability of the ECM-ALGS scaffold for supporting chondrogenic differentiation and underscore its potential as a promising platform for developing novel therapeutic approaches in CTE.

title: Polydatin-loaded PECL microspheres attenuate intervertebral disc degeneration by modulating MGP-associated Ca2+ homeostasis and endoplasmic reticulum stress
abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is a major cause of low back pain (LBP), and endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS)-mediated apoptosis of nucleus pulposus cells (NPCs) contributes to disease progression. Polydatin (PD) has been reported to suppress ERS, but its application is limited by poor solubility and short local retention. We engineered an amphiphilic PCL–PEG microsphere system (PD@PECL) integrating porous architecture, dual PD retention, and biphasic release for controlled intradiscal delivery. PD@PECL reduced thapsigargin-induced ERS, apoptosis, and extracellular matrix degradation in NPCs and showed stronger protective effects than free PD. In a needle puncture-induced rat IVDD model, PD@PECL markedly improved intervertebral disc height, MRI signal intensity, and histological scores. Mechanistically, transcriptomic analysis identified Matrix Gla Protein (MGP) as a PD-responsive mediator. PD increased MGP expression alongside reduced intracellular Ca 2+ accumulation and ERS signaling, whereas siRNA-mediated Mgp knockdown partially attenuated these effects, supporting a functional contribution of MGP. These findings demonstrate that the therapeutic performance of PD@PECL arises from the integration of microsphere engineering, dual-retention design, controlled release, and MGP-associated cellular protection, supporting its potential as a locally retained delivery platform for IVDD treatment.

title: Ceramic metallized Al2O3/Cu heat dissipation architecture for thermopile based thin film heat flux sensor
abstract: Accurate heat-flux measurement is required for reliable thermal load assessment in harsh environments. However, conventional thin-film heat flux sensor (TFHFs) often suffer from limited output voltage and heat accumulation under high thermal loads, leading to overheating and performance degradation. A ceramic metallized TFHFs with peripheral copper heat-dissipation layer was designed and fabricated. Finite element simulations demonstrated that increasing the heat sink height reduced the sensor surface temperature, but the cooling benefit gradually diminished. Therefore, 50 mm was selected by considering thermal performance and structural integration. To reduce interfacial thermal resistance, ceramic metallization combined with brazing was employed to achieve reliable metallurgical bonding between the Al 2 O 3 ceramic substrate and the copper heat sink. A thermopile composed of 29 pairs of NiCr-NiSi thin-film thermocouples was deposited by magnetron sputtering, together with 2000 nm annular thermal resistance layer to establish stable temperature gradient. Static, dynamic, high-temperature durability, and repeatability tests showed that the developed TFHFs exhibited a sensitivity of 0.03715 mV/(kW/m 2 ), a response time of 2.8 ms, and a repeatability error of 3.96%. Vacuum radiation experiments conducted in a space simulation chamber further confirmed stable millivolt-level output and reproducible responses under radiation-dominated heat transfer conditions, demonstrating potential for aerospace heat-flux monitoring

title: A dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for predicting tensile strength retention of FRP composites at elevated temperatures
abstract: Accurate prediction of tensile strength retention (TSR) of fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites exposed to elevated temperatures is essential for assessing their thermal reliability. However, existing ML approaches for TSR prediction have mainly focused on classical algorithms, while recent tabular foundation models and adaptive ensemble strategies remain unexplored. This study addresses these gaps by developing a dynamic Mixture of Experts (MOE) framework using 671 experimental results collected from 26 studies and ten materials, manufacturing, and thermal-exposure variables. Eighteen ML algorithms were systematically evaluated after preprocessing and hyperparameter optimization using grid search with 5-fold cross-validation. TabPFN achieved the best model performance on the independent test set, with an MAE of 2.960, R 2 of 96.788 %, and RMSE of 4.204. To overcome limitations of fixed ensemble methods, five high-performing algorithms (AdaBoost, CatBoost, GBM, RF, and XGBoost) were integrated as experts within a sample-specific dynamic MOE framework. Expert reliability was estimated using training-derived out-of-fold errors, enabling adaptive inverse-error-based weighting without using test target values. Evaluation of 26 expert combinations showed that MOE 1, combining AdaBoost and CatBoost, achieved an MAE of 2.629, R 2 of 96.788 %, and RMSE of 4.204. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach for predicting thermal degradation behavior of heterogeneous FRP composites.

title: Rapid low-energy formation of conductive beaded structures via Joule heating
abstract: Nanoparticle-based pastes are used on a scale of thousands of tons annually to fabricate conductive microtracks, particularly in printed electronics and photovoltaics. However, their high material cost, environmental burden, supply-chain dependence, and limited conductivity create strong demand for sustainable alternatives. Beaded chains of metallic microspheres could address these limitations, but they require post-processing to achieve high conductivity. Here, we investigate localized Joule heating as an efficient route for joining metallic microspheres aligned side by side. We first examined monodisperse microsphere pairs. Experiments focused on neck formation, localized melting, and transient current overshoots, while simulations captured the interplay between current flow, thermal gradients, and liquid–solid phase transitions. The simulations revealed that the initial electrical contact size determines both the maximum temperature and cooling dynamics of the junction. The approach was then extended to beaded chains to assess conductive path formation beyond a single particle pair. Experiments demonstrated rapid conductive joining, while simulations predicted microsecond neck growth. Low energy input is sufficient because heating is concentrated near interparticle contacts rather than throughout the particles. Controlled Joule heating with inexpensive power supplies can tune geometry and resistance in single-particle-thick conductive microtracks, highlighting the potential of this approach for low-cost fabrication.

title: Material–interface trade-offs in biomaterial-based femoral head reconstruction for osteonecrosis: A finite element comparison
abstract: Early stability after femoral head reconstruction reflects implant stiffness, interface fixation, and load-transfer geometry, yet these effects are difficult to separate clinically. We compared four reconstructions in one computed tomography–derived femur with heterogeneous bone properties and a standardised weight-bearing lesion (∼35% of femoral-head volume). Heel strike (HS), mid-stance (MS), and toe-off (TO) were simulated for an isolated fibular strut, screw-augmented strut, porous tantalum rod, and porous β-tricalcium phosphate rod. The screw-augmented strut produced the lowest displacement (1.393–2.108 mm) and subchondral stress (92.3–125.3 MPa), whereas the isolated strut had the lowest mean micromotion (0.080 mm). The β-tricalcium phosphate rod had the lowest implant tensile stress (1.109–1.994 MPa) but the greatest displacement and micromotion. In the tantalum model, increasing interface friction from 0.2 to 0.5 reduced micromotion by 9.4–13.7%, while displacement and subchondral stress changed by < 0.2%. Scenario weighting favoured the screw-augmented strut for collapse resistance and the isolated strut for interface stability. Within this standardised model, performance reflected trade-offs among support, fixation, and material stress rather than stiffness alone. Experimental validation and patient-specific modelling remain necessary before clinical translation.

title: Molecularly integrated Fe-assisted mechanochemical carbon reconstruction and strengthening in graphene/copper composites
abstract: Graphene/copper (Gr/Cu) composites have attracted extensive attention for overcoming the limited mechanical strength of Cu while retaining high electrical conductivity. In-situ conversion of carbon precursors can form graphene-rich reinforcement in Cu, but incomplete conversion leaves amorphous carbon and limits strengthening. Mechanochemical processing provides an alternative in-situ route, yet carbon reconstruction remains limited by insufficient dehydrogenation and C H bond activation. Here, ferrocene was selected as a molecularly integrated Fe-containing precursor for Gr/Cu composites. Cyclopentadiene (CPD) and terphenyl were used as metal-free cyclopentadienyl-ligand (Cp) and mechanochemical carbon-source references, respectively. Compared with CPD and terphenyl, ferrocene produced graphene-rich reinforcement with less amorphous carbon and fewer structural defects after consolidation. Molecular dynamics simulations qualitatively suggest that the Fe center assists Cp-ring opening and carbon-framework reconstruction under shear loading. The ferrocene-derived composite shows a 54% higher yield strength than the CPD-derived composite and nearly twice that of the terphenyl-derived composite. Strengthening analysis attributes this improvement mainly to a larger load-transfer-related contribution from higher-quality graphene-rich reinforcement. An external nano-Fe/CPD control further shows that physically introduced nano Fe species, at an identical Fe/C ratio, do not reproduce the ferrocene-derived carbon reconstruction and strengthening behavior, highlighting the key role of molecular Fe-Cp integration.

title: From percolation to practice: reliable self-sensing ultra high-performance concrete for smart buildings and infrastructure
abstract: The integration of sensing capability into construction materials is essential for developing next-generation smart buildings and infrastructure. Self-sensing ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) is a notable example that combines superior mechanical properties with an inherent electromechanical response. This article reviews self-sensing UHPC, focusing on materials design, the formation of conductive networks, manufacturing techniques, and the performance of the concrete as a sensor. Emphasis is placed on changes in the electromechanical response under various loading types, including compression, tension, flexural, cyclic, and fatigue loading, as well as changes in the continuity of the conductive networks. Advanced techniques in the electrical characterization of materials, measurement configurations, and the processing of signals associated with sensing reliability are also reviewed. Compared with conventional self-sensing concrete, UHPC exhibits enhanced structural robustness, reduced environmental sensitivity, and improved damage detection capability despite moderate strain sensitivity. The current limitations in standardization, durability, and large-scale implementation are highlighted, and directions are proposed to advance self-sensing UHPC toward reliable, scalable structural health monitoring applications

title: Biomechanical evaluation of screw-supported prostheses in reconstructing Paprosky IIIB acetabular defects
abstract: Paprosky IIIB acetabular defects represent one of the most severe forms of bone loss, often reconstructed using custom-made triflange acetabular components (CTAC). However, traditional CTACs might exhibit insufficient stability under extensive bone loss. Building on the use of long column screws in acetabular reconstruction, this study proposed and biomechanically evaluated a screw-supported acetabular prosthesis based on pile-foundation principles for the reconstruction of Paprosky IIIB acetabular defects. Based on defect morphology, three implants were modeled: a standard triflange cup, an enhanced triflange cup and a screw-supported prosthesis. Finite element analysis (FEA) was conducted under three physiological loading conditions: walking, stair ascent, and stair descent. Von Mises stress, bone strain, and interface micromotion were used to assess mechanical performance. Mechanical compression tests validated the FEA results. The results indicated that the screw-supported prosthesis showed lower, more evenly distributed stresses, a broader strain area within the bone regeneration range, and smaller micromotion in posterior column defects. In anterior column defects, it demonstrated lower peak stresses and improved micromotion. Biomechanical experimental results aligned with the FEA outcomes. This design provided a biomechanically solution for individualized acetabular reconstruction, particularly for posterior column defects, and validated the application of pile foundation principles in orthopedic implant design.

title: A coupled crystal plasticity-damage RVE framework for predicting macroscopic ductile fracture locus
abstract: Predicting the macroscopic ductile fracture locus of sheet metals directly from microstructural simulations remains challenging. This work develops a coupled crystal plasticity–damage framework that links a slip-system-level continuum damage model with a representative volume element (RVE) failure criterion, enabling direct construction of the macroscopic fracture locus from virtual experiments on AA6061-T6 alloy. Implemented in the DAMASK spectral solver, the damage model introduces four parameters governing damage rate, stress-state sensitivity, slip-history nonlinearity, and the incubation threshold. A multi-grain void-cluster connectivity criterion is proposed to define RVE failure without relying on numerical termination. The damage parameters are calibrated using uniaxial and plane-strain tension fracture strains from the modified Mohr–Coulomb (MMC3) locus and then tested under four proportional stress states from simple shear to equibiaxial tension. The framework reproduces the characteristic U-shaped fracture locus, with maximum deviations of approximately 28% under shear and 10% under equibiaxial tension. Without recalibration, it also predicts pronounced texture sensitivity: the Cube texture increases the uniaxial fracture strain by about 47%, whereas the Brass texture suppresses the tensile peak, with fracture strains remaining between 0.2 and 0.5 for positive triaxialities. The framework therefore provides a microstructure-informed route for generating texture-sensitive fracture loci for macroscopic forming simulations.

title: Acoustic impedance Compensation: A Materials-Centric heuristic for Next-Generation ultrasound molecular imaging
abstract: Background Ultrasonic molecular imaging (UMI) uses targeted microbubbles and nanoparticles for early diagnosis and therapy. However, its clinical application is hampered by biosafety uncertainties and performance variability due to biological heterogeneity.Consequently, we introduce a heuristic Acoustic Impedance Compensation (AIC) framework, inspired by materials science, to navigate the core sensitivity-stability trade-off . Objective This narrative review proposes a design paradigm of targeted UMI agents in cancer and inflammatory diseases. It also explores the utility of the AIC framework and an evidence gap analysis for interpreting contradictory reports and guiding future inquiry. Methods We synthesized literature from major databases (inception to December 2025), encompassing in vitro, animal, and human studies. Given methodological diversity, a qualitative synthesis was performed, interpreting findings through the AIC perspective. Results The aggregated evidence suggests UMI may enhance early detection sensitivity in some contexts. The AIC framework provides a plausible model for anomalous data, proposing that dynamic impedance modulation could stabilize signals in heterogeneous tissues. Persistent challenges include biosafety and production inconsistencies. Conclusions Targeted agents appear to advance UMI. The AIC framework proposes a novel design paradigm to overcome sensitivity-stability limits. Therefore, future work should prioritize validating this model through integrated analysis and clinical trials to enable reliable personalized applications.

title: Waste-derived precursors for transition-metal alloys, carbides and MAX phases: a critical review of specification, purification burden and end-use requirements
abstract: Most of the cost and embodied energy of precursors for the early transition metals, aluminium, silicon and carbon arises in refining to a specified grade rather than in extraction. Industrial and agricultural residues contain these elements, yet their use is usually assessed as a recovery problem rather than a specification problem. This review develops a specification and cost-based framework for determining when waste-derived precursors can substitute for primary feedstocks. Purification ladders linking form, attainable purity and price are compiled for each element; for titanium, indicative price rises more than tenfold from ilmenite to sponge metal and again to classified powder. Impurity budgets for the principal end-uses are used to evaluate recovery routes from metallurgical slags, bauxite residue, spent catalysts, aluminium dross, silica fume, rice-husk ash and carbonaceous residues. At equal specification, provenance alone does not determine performance or cost; secondary feedstocks are competitive when the residue has already undergone part of the primary processing, when the end-use accepts feed from a lower rung of the ladder, or when avoided disposal costs are material. These conditions are met industrially for vanadium from steelmaking slag and for secondary aluminium, and in principle for carbides made carbothermically from oxide feed. Layered ternary carbides and nitrides (MAX phases) are examined as a stringent specification case: their impurity tolerance is site-specific, and carbide or oxycarbide intermediates are more compatible with residue-derived titanium than titanium dioxide. For several end-uses, adoption appears limited less by attainable purity than by the absence of certified, batch-consistent specifications

title: High-throughput preparation of microdroplet arrays by multi-channel electrohydrodynamic printing
abstract: Electrohydrodynamic (EHD) printing technology was well recognized for its high resolution and excellent material compatibility. Nevertheless, conventional single-nozzle EHD printing was constrained by low throughput. Multi-channel EHD printing was developed to overcome this limitation, but jet deflection and interruption were induced by electric-field coupling among nozzles, which degraded printing accuracy and microdroplet array uniformity. In this paper, a multi-physics coupling model was established to compare the electric field distributions of three typical nozzle array configurations. The simulation results revealed that a large electric field gradient could be generated by the single-row linear distribution. Based on this, a multi-channel spinneret with auxiliary electrodes was further designed. The spatial electric field distribution was optimized and the repulsive effects between jets were reduced through the introduction of solid nozzles. The influences of key process parameters, on jet stability and droplet deposition morphology were systematically investigated. Microdroplet arrays with average droplet diameters of 344–380 μm and printing frequencies of 198–324 Hz were successfully fabricated with the multi-channel spinneret with auxiliary electrodes. High-throughput preparation of microdroplet arrays was achieved through synergistic parameter optimization, and a feasible manufacturing solution for applications in flexible displays was thereby provided.

title: Fabrication and high-temperature response mechanism of Pt/PtRh10 curved-surface thermocouples via 3D direct writing
abstract: Conformal thermocouples are required for in-situ temperature monitoring of high-temperature components with complex geometries, while the influence of specific geometric configurations on thermoelectric response remains insufficiently understood. Here, Pt/PtRh10 thermocouples were fabricated on planar and curved-surface alumina substrates via 3D direct-writing technology. Microstructural characterization confirmed that different geometric configurations did not induce detectable changes in the phase structure or composition of the thermoelectric films. Multiphysics simulations and calibration experiments demonstrated highly consistent thermoelectric responses between different configurations, with sensitivities of 9.31 and 9.33 μV/°C, respectively. The fabricated devices maintained stable operation at 1303.15 °C for 18 h. The observed measurement deviation was attributed primarily to geometry-dependent thermal boundary conditions rather than intrinsic changes in thermoelectric properties. A geometry-specific equivalent Seebeck coefficient compensation model was developed to correct configuration-dependent measurement deviations, enabling accurate temperature monitoring for complex high-temperature structures.

title: Implantation-driven metastable polymorph engineering and local silicon coordination in Ga2O3
abstract: Ion implantation in gallium oxide (Ga 2 O 3 ) can both introduce dopants and kinetically trap non-equilibrium polymorphs. We investigate how implantation temperature governs polymorph formation, silicon localization, and long-term structural stability in Si-implanted β-Ga 2 O 3 (100). Room-temperature implantation produces pronounced disorder and drives a disorder-mediated β → γ transformation, which is unambiguously identified by HR XRD. In contrast, implantation at 625 °C promotes dynamic defect recovery and preserves a predominantly β-Ga 2 O 3 structure. Si K-edge XANES shows that Si is predominantly present as Si 4+ but adopts polymorph-dependent local environments. In β-Ga 2 O 3 , Si is distributed between substitutional donor sites and interstitial, defect-associated configurations with γ-like coordination. In γ-Ga 2 O 3 , the Si-related contribution is preferentially associated with the intrinsically partially occupied nonspinel cation sublattice of the defective-spinel structure. A substantial Si fraction also exhibits SiO 2 -like coordination, consistent with partial chemical segregation and the formation of a nanoscale oxide composite within the implanted layer. After approximately one year of ambient storage, samples initially retaining predominantly β-type long-range order develop weak γ-related diffraction signatures, demonstrating delayed structural evolution of the implantation-modified state. These results show that implantation temperature, local dopant coordination, kinetic trapping, and time-dependent defect evolution must be considered together when designing implantation and subsequent thermal processing routes for Ga 2 O 3 -based materials.

title: Vancomycin-loaded quasi-MOF thermosensitive hydrogels for synergistic anti-inflammatory and healing of infected wounds
abstract: Effective clinical management of infected wounds remains challenging due to the transient efficacy and resistance-inducing nature of conventional antibiotics. Multifunctional dressings capable of sustained drug release and microenvironment modulation are urgently needed. Herein, we present a smart thermosensitive hydrogel based on metal–organic framework nanozymes and an antibacterial agent, integrating vancomycin-loaded quasi-MIL-53 (Van@QMIL-53) into a biocompatible chitosan network to form a synergistic triple-action antibacterial system (VQCG). QMIL-53 exhibits enhanced catalytic activity and drug-loading capacity. The chitosan matrix enables sustained drug release and provides ideal wound management properties, including thermosensitivity, excellent swelling capacity, antioxidant activity, and skin adhesion. In vitro, the hydrogel demonstrates potent antibacterial activity against P. aeruginosa and methicillin-resistant S. aureus ( MRSA ). In vivo, its therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in a murine model of wounds co-infected with MRSA and P. aeruginosa. The hydrogel significantly accelerated wound healing by simultaneously eradicating pathogens, scavenging excess reactive oxygen species, and alleviating inflammation, as evidenced by downregulated Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α) and upregulated Arginase-1 (Arg-1) expression. This work establishes a versatile MOF-hydrogel platform, offering a promising strategy for advanced wound dressings that synergistically address infection, oxidative stress, and tissue repair.

title: Turbulence induced shear-assisted and continuous synthesis of micro-sized silver flakes in Taylor-Couette flows
abstract: The present study has demonstrated that the nanoparticle seed crystal growth direction is strongly influenced by the local turbulence induced shear rate. A continuous flow synthesis process for synthesis of the silver flakes without adopting the seed mediation and structure-directing agents in turbulent Taylor-Couette flow was particularly studied. Turbulence induced shear controllable synthesis experiments were conducted using a specially designed Taylor-Couette flow reactor (TCFR) to investigate the effects of operation temperature and shear rate on the formation of silver flakes with the experimental data being compared with those by intermittent reactive synthesis using a conventional beaker. The turbulence induced shear Reynolds stresses in the flows of both reactors were evaluated by using the Reynolds Stress Model (RSM), identifying the correlations between the turbulence induced shear and orientation of silver flakes. It was revealed that the use of TCFR for synthesis of silver flakes is conducive to the synthesis of silver flakes compared to the use of beaker. An increase in the operation temperature can help to deliver smoother flake surfaces. The numerical modelling results clearly show that the local turbulence induced shear taking place in the TCFR is very likely the decisive factor affecting silver flake generation.

title: Multi-objective design and validation of a bioinspired tri-zonal scaffold for tendon-bone interfaces
abstract: The tendon-bone interface exhibits a complex gradient in mechanical and morphological properties, enabling robust load transfer between soft and hard tissues. Replicating this functionality in engineered scaffolds remains challenging. Here, we present a computational-experimental framework for developing tri-zonal scaffolds with spatially varying stiffness and zone-specific architectures for tendon-bone interface applications. A hybrid lattice combining strut-based and surface-based geometries was used to generate tendon-like, transitional, and bone-like zones. Homogenization-based modeling and 3D finite element simulations were used to screen 36 feasible design configurations. Two representative designs were fabricated via fused deposition modeling and integrated with an alginate-gelatin hydrogel. Micro-computed tomography was used to assess manufacturing fidelity, and identify architecture-dependent geometric deviations, while mechanical testing characterized the response of the fabricated scaffolds and hydrogel-integrated constructs. Design A exhibited a 72–93% higher maximum tensile force than Design B, with failure observed predominantly within the hydrogel adjacent to the scaffold-hydrogel interface. Preliminary in vitro observations with MC3T3-E1 preosteoblasts showed qualitative differences in cell morphology and spatial organization between scaffold architectures and zones. These findings demonstrate the use of a multi-objective design framework for integrating zone-specific mechanical and morphological requirements and provide a basis for further development of engineered soft-hard tissue interfaces.

title: Mode-dependent effects of PCB surface finishes on multiband bandpass filter performance
abstract: Demand for high-speed multiband RF circuits has increased, driven by the demand for high-speed data transmission, enhanced connectivity, multi-band operations, and miniaturized devices. Owing to manufacturing requirements, these devices are coated with surface finishes. The key purpose of surface coating materials is to shield the underlying copper from oxidation and guarantee long-term reliability. Regardless, they significantly influence the electrical properties of conductors. This work focuses on the impact of PCB surface finishes on the performance of a high-frequency multiband bandpass filter designed for space-based asset applications, with particular attention to mode-dependent mechanisms. To this end, different metallization configurations are investigated on the copper profile. Upon analysis, resonant frequencies, bandwidths, and midband isolation remain largely unchanged. Nevertheless, significant degradations in insertion loss and resonator quality factor are distinguished, particularly for ENIG finish. The results reveal non-monotonic behavior, and variations do not follow a traditional frequency-scaling (√f) trend. Instead, they exhibit strong mode-dependent current-distribution behavior within the structure. Each band corresponds to a distinct resonant mode with electromagnetic field localization. These findings demonstrate that conventional frequency-dependent surface resistance models remain inadequate for predicting conductor losses in multiband filters, providing new design insights for RF component optimization in advanced multiband communication systems.

title: Effects of Mg and Mn contents on the mechanical properties, corrosion behavior, and biocompatibility of biomedical zinc alloys
abstract: Zinc-based alloys are promising biodegradable implant materials, but their mechanical, corrosion, and biological properties require coordinated optimization. Here, Zn-Mg-Mn alloys with varying Mg and Mn contents were fabricated by powder metallurgy and evaluated for microstructure, mechanical properties, corrosion, wear, and biological performance. Zn-2.5 Mg-3.5Mn achieved the highest compressive yield strength (360 MPa) in the Zn-2.5 Mg-xMn series. Increasing Mn from 0 to 3.5 wt% raised hardness from 85 to 105 HV, while high-alloy-content specimens showed over 50 % lower wear rates. Among the ternary alloys, Zn-2.5 Mg-1Mn had the lowest electrochemical equivalent corrosion rate from short-term potentiodynamic polarization (0.375 mm/y). All alloys exhibited grade 0 cytotoxicity and hemolysis below 5 %. Zn-2.5 Mg-1Mn supported relatively high osteoblast viability and showed lower absolute BSA and fibrinogen adsorption, although cell adhesion and spreading were limited. Short-term subcutaneous implantation in mice caused mild early inflammation, followed by tissue repair and remodeling by day 7, without extensive ulceration or necrosis. Overall, Zn-2.5 Mg-1Mn provided a favorable balance of mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, in vitro biocompatibility, and short-term tissue response, supporting its potential as a biodegradable implant material.

title: Innovative advances in intelligent droplet microfluidics: from machine vision-augmented quantifications to autonomous control
abstract: Droplet microfluidics has emerged as a powerful platform for high-throughput chemical and biological processing, offering precise control over multiphase flows, minimal reagent consumption, and scalable operation. However, accurate prediction and control of droplet formation remain fundamentally challenging because droplet breakup is governed by strongly coupled, nonlinear interactions among interfacial tension, viscous forces, flow conditions, and microchannel geometry that abruptly switch between distinct regimes. Conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and semi-empirical scaling laws not only incur prohibitive computational cost but, more critically, fail to generalize across geometries and break down for complex fluids, surfactant-laden interfaces, non-Newtonian rheology, and cannot perform the inverse design or real-time control that practical devices demand. Artificial intelligence (AI) directly addresses these intractable problems by learning high-dimensional, nonlinear mappings from data without explicit governing equations. Machine learning and deep learning predict droplet characteristics, classify flow regimes, and analyze high-speed imaging orders of magnitude faster than CFD, while reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization enable closed-loop control and autonomous experimentation unattainable by conventional means. This review surveys AI integration across predictive modeling, intelligent flow control, and automated design, and discusses emerging opportunities and key challenges, data scarcity, model generalization, and system integration, toward autonomous, intelligent microfluidic laboratories.

title: On the design of isotropic periodic material
abstract: Elastic isotropy is a fundamental constitutive characteristic of architected periodic materials, requiring the effective mechanical response to be invariant with loading direction. Designing microstructures with prescribed isotropic properties is therefore a stringent inverse problem. However, isotropic constitutive responses obtained through topology optimisation may not be preserved after geometric realisation and high-fidelity analysis, owing to discrepancies in geometric reconstruction and numerical evaluation. To address this issue, this study develops a what-you-see-is-what-you-get (WYSIWYG) topology optimisation framework that maintains consistency between the optimised geometry and its high-fidelity CAD reconstruction while improving the accuracy of constitutive response evaluation. A hypersurface-based representation with an exact material boundary enables faithful CAD reconstruction without altering the optimised geometry, while a two-stage optimisation strategy with fine-mesh re-optimisation and exact integration improves the accuracy of the homogenised constitutive response. The framework is demonstrated through the optimisation of shear modulus, bulk modulus, and Poisson’s ratio under isotropy constraints. The resulting designs exhibit highly isotropic effective properties that remain consistent after CAD reconstruction and independent high-fidelity finite-element evaluation. Physical experiments on selected fabricated designs provide additional support for their isotropic mechanical response.

title: Highly precise and efficient simulation of large-scale conformal lattice structure based on residual fully connected neural network
abstract: Conformal lattices are recognized as ideal lightweight materials for curved aerospace structures such as wing skins due to geometric adaptability and spatial utilization. However, the billions of FE meshes generated by millions of lattice structures increase the cost of simulation, and the current homogenization methods for conformal lattices have difficulty convincing accuracy. A simulation method for large-scale conformal lattice structure based on residual fully connected neural network (R-FCNN) is proposed. An isoparametric mapping homogenization method based on voxelized cells are developed. A prediction model based on R-FCNN is constructed to achieve the equivalent performance. By replacing the conformal lattice with a hexahedron made of an anisotropic material, the simulation efficiency is improved while simulation accuracy is maintained.
